title: Crit Happens
use_cases: Use when designing a tabletop RPG dungeon centered on psychological horror
Implement when creating a gameplay loop that rewards risks with gradual narrative discovery
Configure when balancing game mechanics to foster a sense of powerlessness or dread
Use when leveraging established horror tropes to manage player expectations in D&D
content:
This, I found, leads to the cornerstone of what makes horror: dread.

Dread relies on this disempowerment. In film, we see ignorant jocks heading down into the basement despite warning signs, and we scream because we cannot stop them. Dread is a slow build. With each step, the jock inches closer to certain doom, and we must endure the agony of seeing it coming, but being powerless to save them. That is dread, that feeling of knowing something terrible is coming, but not being able to deal with it until it is upon you.

As the characters explore my location, they’ll quickly come to understand that it is more than a loose collection of ghouls and spiders. They’ll intuit there are much darker forces at work, that there is a reason these things are happening. Without understanding it completely, they have little hope of escaping. But the only way to learn more is to explore deeper, knowing that the dark forces will resist harder the deeper they delve. This is the way in which I aim achieve dread across my adventure.

Much like people sitting down with a bowl of popcorn to watch the latest slasher flick, players will come to the table with certain expectations. They know their characters likely won’t make it out in one piece. They know there will be traps, and scary monsters, and diabolical puzzles. And they are willing to accept these things, as long as they are provided thrills in return. By evoking that sense of dread that slowly builds to a terrifying crescendo, while delivering the unexpected along the way, and forcing the players out of their characters’ comfort zones, I hope to reward them handsomely.

Dungeons & Dragons does not lend itself well to horror, no. But horror lends itself well to Dungeons & Dragons players if we are only willing to buy in heavily to the tried-and-true, well-loved tropes of the genre. This Halloween, when I release Malevolence Manor, I hope to be proven right.
